{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-in-s","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"725e84713c6f92aea9cf0cf8c99060521ebfffc96ded08689bf01294ca76cea1","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-in-class-std:lineage:23","source_registry_sha256":"2800087d52ca58455ac6dac735a6e1bd60a4442f9e09c2356d96bd9ed8102504","source_liveness_sha256":"4d2b75b9a10fb774f53fb2d906a3a7a7f75f5e9387f8b4ddcd423e9b7828d59b"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Traffic sign colors and shapes, traffic signals, right of way at signs and signals, and pedestrian signals","heading":"C — Sign colors, sign shapes, the slow-moving vehicle emblem, steady and flashing signals, turning on green and red, stop lines, yield signs, dark signals and pedestrian signals","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Sign colors, sign shapes, the slow-moving vehicle emblem, steady and flashing signals, turning on green and red, stop lines, yield signs, dark signals and pedestrian signals
Knowledge domain: how Indiana traffic signs use background color and shape to tell a driver what kind of message they carry, what each steady, flashing or arrow signal means for right of way, how to turn legally on a green or a red, where to stop at a red light or stop sign, what to do at a yield sign or a dark signal, and how pedestrian signals and beacons work. Facts below come from the manual's written text only, never from the sign pictures.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Indiana traffic signs are put up by the Indiana Department of Transportation and local governments, and they rely on colors, shapes, written messages and symbols so drivers can grasp them quickly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
A brown sign points to a nearby recreational or cultural site, such as a state park. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
A blue sign gives road services and information, such as the amenities at an upcoming exit. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
A green sign shows permitted movements, directions or guidance, such as highway entrances and exits or the distance to destinations ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
An orange sign warns of temporary traffic conditions, most often from highway construction or maintenance work ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
A white sign shows regulations a driver must obey, such as speed limits, and also carries helpful information like state highway markers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
A yellow sign prepares drivers for specific road conditions and hazards ahead and can alert them to a nearby school zone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
A fluorescent yellow-green sign warns of nearby schools, pedestrians, bicycles, playgrounds and school bus routes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A01
A red sign carries a regulation that demands immediate action to avoid a safety threat, with the Wrong Way sign given as an example. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
A circular sign warns that a railroad crossing is coming up. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A02
A triangle sign with three equal sides tells drivers to slow down near an intersection and be ready to stop fully to yield to other drivers or pedestrians. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A02
A pennant-shaped sign is posted on the left side of a two-way road to warn drivers not to pass vehicles on the left. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A02
A rectangular sign can show a regulation such as a speed limit, helpful information such as a route marker, or a hazard warning such as an advisory speed for a sharp curve. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
A diamond-shaped sign warns of road conditions and hazards ahead, such as a road that is slippery when wet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
A five-sided sign warns that you are entering an area near a school where children may be crossing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A02
An eight-sided sign tells drivers they must stop and yield the proper right of way at the intersection. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A04
The slow-moving vehicle emblem has a fluorescent orange center and red reflective borders and marks a vehicle that cannot go faster than 25 miles per hour. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A07
Facing a green light, you have the right of way and may go through the intersection as long as it is clear of vehicles and pedestrians. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A07
A steady yellow light means the green has ended and red is coming; if you are already too close to stop safely, you may finish your movement. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A07
Facing a red light, you must stop and may not enter the intersection until your light turns green and the intersection is clear, because cross traffic has the right of way. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A08
A green arrow shown with a red or green light gives you the right of way to make that turn as long as the intersection is clear. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A08
On a green light with no arrow you may turn when the intersection is clear but must yield to all oncoming traffic, and only one vehicle at a time may enter to turn left. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A08
A flashing yellow turn arrow lets you turn only after you have yielded to pedestrians and oncoming traffic. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A08
Where a right turn on red is allowed, you must stop fully, check that no vehicles or pedestrians are in or entering your path, confirm there is no No Turn on Red sign, and use the correct lane. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A08
A left turn on a red light or arrow is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after the same full stop and checks as a right turn on red. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A08
A flashing yellow light with no arrow means slow down and use caution; cross-street traffic must yield to you, but a left turn still requires yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A08
A flashing red light at an intersection counts as a stop sign: come to a complete stop, then go ahead with caution. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A08
At a flashing red where all directions must stop, yield to vehicles already in the intersection and to those that stopped first; if two drivers arrive together, the one on the left yields. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A09
At a red light or stop sign, stop at the solid white stop line; with no stop line, stop before the crosswalk on your side, and with no crosswalk, stop before entering the intersection. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A09
A yield sign means slow down and be ready to stop fully, and a driver with the right of way coming from another direction should never need to brake to avoid you. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A09
At an intersection whose signal is not working, stop first, then go only after yielding to cross traffic already inside, to vehicles that stopped before you, to vehicles arriving with you on your right, and to pedestrians. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A10
A pedestrian signal showing WALK or a walking person means pedestrians may cross safely, and some crossings have a push button to call the walk signal. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A10
A DON'T WALK message or raised hand means it is not safe to cross, and when it flashes the safe crossing time is running out. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A10
A pedestrian hybrid beacon stays dark until a pedestrian activates it, then shows flashing yellow, steady yellow, two steady reds during the crossing, and flashing reds that let drivers go if the crossing is clear. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

Misconceptions: a flashing red is not a slow-down signal, it requires a full stop like a stop sign; a green light without an arrow does not give left-turners priority over oncoming traffic; a left on red is never allowed from a two-way street; a steady yellow is not a signal to speed up, it only lets you finish when you are too close to stop safely; white regulation signs are rules, not suggestions.
Mnemonics: eight sides means stop, three sides means yield, five sides means school, round means railroad, pennant means no passing; orange is for work zones, brown is for parks, blue is for services, green is for guidance.
Glossary: right of way means the legal priority to proceed first; pennant means a sideways triangular sign on the left side of a two-way road; advisory speed means a recommended speed for a curve, ramp or exit; pedestrian hybrid beacon means a mid-block crossing signal that stays dark until a pedestrian activates it; stop line means the solid white line where a vehicle stops.
Dynamic facts: none in these pages; sign designs and signal rules are stable rules of the road, and no fees, phone numbers or service details appear.
